newsitem.title: USA: Labor urges Clinton to push on workers rights.
newsitem.headline: Labor urges Clinton to push on workers rights.

text.p: International labor leaders asked President Bill Clinton on Monday to urge other leaders of the rich industrial nations to make labor and human rights issues a part of international trade and investment agreements.

"Global trade was suppose to bring benefits to the whole world. That is how it was advertised and yet it is a fact that unemployment and insecurity are on the increase around the world," Bill Jordan, general secretary of the International Confederation of Free Trade Unions, told reporters following a White House meeting with Clinton.

The labor leaders, who included AFL-CIO President John Sweeney, asked Clinton to present a joint statement on labor issues and globalization at the upcoming meeting of leaders of the Group of Seven rich industrial nations.
"We had a cordial and very helpful exchange of ideas," Sweeney said. "We're sure the president will be supportive of our joint statement."
"There is a desperate need for new rules to help manage the global change that is upon us and to guarantee that workers and their families share in the gains they help produce," he added.

White House officials said it was traditional for the leaders of countries hosting the annual gathering of the G7 to meet labor leaders ahead of the summit. The United States is hosting the G7 meeting June 20-21 in Denver.

The issue of workers rights and trade agreements was highly controversial at the December meeting of World Trade Organization trade ministers. Also Clinton's efforts to have labor issues included in trade negotiation legislation has met stiff resistance among Republicans in control of Congress.
Labor groups argued that it is only fair to protect workers as well as capital and property in trade agreements.

"We have agreements on intellectual property rights, agreements on investment rights, agreements on trade for multinational corporations and we have no agreements to protect workers rights," said Robert White, president of the Trade Union Advisory Committee of the the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development.
"We believe that Denver must not duck this challenge," added Jordan.

The group of labor leaders also asked Clinton to seek support from his G7 counterparts for the release of jailed Indonesian labor leader Muchtar Pakpahan. He was arrestd last year after deadly riots in Indonesia.
